MBMM · 22nm Memristor-Based Main Memory

Can 22nm ReRAM Replace
DDR5 in a Commodity DIMM?

Evaluation of 22nm Memristor-Based Main Memory (MBMM) in Commodity DIMM Architectures

Yuval Kogan · Advisor: Prof. Shahar Kvatinsky · September 2026
01
Section 01

Motivation

Why system-level ReRAM, why now

Motivation1 / 4

The Memory Supply-Demand Crisis

  • Late 2025: DRAM wafer capacity reallocated to HBM for AI accelerators
  • Commodity main memory supply is getting squeezed by that shift
  • The question this creates: what else can serve as a DRAM alternative in standard DIMMs?
SayDRAM capacity is being pulled toward AI/HBM; commodity main memory is getting squeezed. That's the market pressure motivating alternatives.
Motivation2 / 4

Why ReRAM as a Candidate

  • Non-volatile - zero refresh power, by construction
  • Density potential - resistive cells can beat a scaling-limited DRAM capacitor
  • Logic-compatible process - fabricable on mature, high-volume CMOS nodes
  • The classic objection: endurance. Flagged now, addressed head-on later.
SayThe pitch is refresh elimination and density - but endurance is the classic objection, flag it now so it doesn't feel dodged later.
Motivation3 / 4

Device-level ReRAM is well studied.

System-level, commodity-DIMM behavior under real workloads is not.

SayMost ReRAM literature stops at the cell or macro. This project asks the system question - what happens when you put it in a DIMM behind a memory controller and run real traces through it.
Motivation4 / 4

What This Project Built

  • A cross-layer pipeline: NVSim (device physics) → NVMain 2.0 (system simulation)
  • Driven by real workload traces - SPEC CPU2017 (gcc, lbm) via gem5, STREAM, AI inference via SCALE-Sim
  • 20 memory configurations × 6 benchmarks
SayThis is the specific, concrete thing being evaluated. The angle is system-level, cross-layer, workload-driven - not a claim of being first-ever.
02
Section 02

Background

The architectures and the yardsticks

Background1 / 4

1T1R vs 1S1R, in One Breath

20F²
1T1R - transistor-gated, no sneak paths, planar access device
4F²
1S1R - selector-gated, smaller cell, slower access path

Cell area is architecture-dependent, not fixed - a DRAM-process recessed-channel 1T1R has hit 6F² in a commercial part.

SayOne sentence recap since the audience already has this; then land on why cell area isn't a fixed constant - the recessed-channel demo is a footnote for the density slide later.
Background2 / 4

SLC vs MLC

  • SLC - 1 bit/cell, single resistance threshold
  • MLC - 2+ bits/cell via Iterative Step-and-Verify (ISPV) programming → write-latency penalty
  • NVSim crashes simulating MLC's iterative sensing natively - this project derived an analytical penalty method from the same EMBER macro's two publications instead (Upton et al., ESSCIRC 2023 [6]; Levy et al., IEEE JSSC 2024 [31])
SayNVSim can't natively simulate MLC's iterative sensing, so this project derived an analytical penalty method from two independent EMBER macro papers instead - sets up a methodology slide.

Every technology here is judged on the same three axes: latency, density, endurance - power is a closely related fourth. When an axis isn't evaluated for a technology, that's a disclosed scope choice, not a missing fact.

*PCM's baseline is a black-box timing/energy model with no stated access-device architecture - neither transistor- nor selector-gated. The real shipped product (Intel Optane/3D XPoint) is a confirmed 1S1R cross-point design, not modeled here.

Methodology

The pipeline, the workloads, the honesty checks

Methodology1 / 8

The Pipeline

1_run_nvsim_hardware.py
NVSim
device characterization
→
2_extract_hardware_metrics.py
Parse → JSON
(+ analytical MLC)
→
3_gen_nvmain_config.py
Replicate chip ×1/8/16/64

NVMain 2.0

Orchestrated end-to-end by mbmm_master.py - “The Gate-Keeper” (Section 2.2)

What actually crosses step 1→2, field by field: coming up shortly (“The Bridge, in Parameters”).

SayNVSim only ever characterizes ONE chip - that's what crosses the boundary at step 1→2. Everything from step 3 onward is NVMain replicating that single chip a small, fixed number of times and wrapping it in its own controller; NVSim never sees a rank, a controller, or a workload. This bridge is itself a contribution - most tools stop at one layer or the other.
Methodology2 / 8

One Chip → a Full DIMM

1 Gb
per-chip capacity (gigabit, not gigabyte; Table 1)
1–64
chips replicated per config - single → 8chip → 16chip → full DIMM
800 MHz
ReRAM device clock (PCM 400 MHz, DDR5 2400 MHz)
64-bit
DIMM bus width
8 / 16 GB
full-DIMM capacity, SLC / MLC (2 bits/cell doubles it)
3 GHz
host CPU issue rate (CPUFreq) - same for ReRAM, PCM, and DDR5; not a device clock

64 × 1 Gb ÷ 8 (bits to bytes) = 8 GB SLC; MLC's 2 bits/cell doubles it to 16 GB. NVMain adds the FRFCFS controller, decoder, and interconnect NVSim has none of.

SayNVSim gives one 1 Gb (gigabit) chip - a cell count, not a byte count; NVMain's controller and address-mapping logic turns up to 64 of them into an 8-16 GB DIMM. The 800 MHz interface is a deliberate choice, not a device limit, and has no independent ReRAM citation backing it - a targeted search found no ReRAM interface-speed paper, and the only real ReRAM chip I/O clocks located (Fujitsu SPI parts, 5-10 MHz) run far slower. Disclosed as a modeling assumption, not a literature-derived figure - costs ground in the bandwidth-bound AI regime, which is why dual-channel/faster-PHY ReRAM is scoped as future work.
Methodology3 / 8

The Bridge, in Parameters

NVSim output (Table 1) [3]

  • Read / write latency (ns)
  • Read / write energy (nJ)
  • Leakage (mW/chip)
  • Die area (mm²), capacity

NVMain input (Appendix B) [4]

  • tCAS / tRCD / tRP (cycles)
  • Erd / Ewr (nJ, per access)
  • Eactstdby / Eprestdby (nJ, per cycle)
  • ROWS / COLS / RANKS / BANKS

Conversion, not new physics: ns to cycles at the target clock; per-chip leakage to per-cycle rank standby energy.

SayThis is what "the bridge" is doing at the field level - not reinterpreting the physics, just unit and granularity conversion. This exact seam is where the toolchain audit found most of its 14 bugs.
Methodology4 / 8

Methodology5 / 8

Baselines

  • DDR5-4800 - modeled strictly to JEDEC JESD79-5 timing & refresh [10] - the real target to beat
  • Legacy PCM (2009) - architectural framing from Lee et al. [11]; inherited timing/energy parameters trace to Choi et al., ISSCC 2012 [41], not run through this project's own NVSim pipeline
SayDDR5 is the real target to beat; PCM shows how far NVM has come. One thing to know cold if asked: PCM is a legacy reference baseline taken as-is from NVMain, not characterized through this project's own NVSim pipeline the way ReRAM is - different methodology, disclosed plainly.
Methodology6 / 8

I Audited My Own Toolchain

14

silent failure modes found in the standard NVSim → NVMain flow - 12 repaired and validated

  • Leakage and access-energy were silently ignored by the power model - wired in and re-run; this is what the 47x leakage gap and the 1.12 W figure rest on
  • DDR5's refresh timing/supply were inherited unscaled from a DDR3-1333 template - corrected to real DDR5-4800 JEDEC values
  • ReRAM's MLC multipliers were unsourced ("EMBER heuristics" not in the cited paper) - re-sourced to Upton et al. [6] / Levy et al. [31], re-derived
  • Idle power-down is still disabled in NVMain's source - found and documented, not yet fixed; every ReRAM figure here is worst-case ungated (top-priority future work)
SayThis is a genuine strength - present it as rigor, not confession. Twelve of fourteen are fixed and re-validated; the two still open (idle power-down, trace provenance) are disclosed, not hidden.
Methodology7 / 8

What “Validated” Means Here

Limitation, stated up front
  • Validation = internal consistency - NVMain reproduces NVSim's own numbers to 0.0% error
  • NOT validation against a real fabricated chip or a measured DDR5 DIMM
SayBe the one who raises this before someone in the audience does.
Methodology8 / 8

Assumptions That Shape Every Result Next

  • gem5 traces are uncached - maximum memory pressure, not real cache-filtered traffic
  • GPT-2 trace provenance is unverified - treated as a representative stress pattern
  • DDR5 power = datasheet spec-limit maxima, not typical values
  • ReRAM power = worst-case, ungated - idle-power gating not yet simulated
SayRead every number in the next 25 minutes through this lens - this slide is the fix for caveats surfacing too late.

Section 04

Results

Latency, power, scaling, and global viability

Results · Latency1 / 4

Compute-Bound: the Closest Gap

  • 1T1R SLC: 136 ns vs DDR5 90 ns
  • A 1.5× gap - the smallest in the suite
Results · Latency2 / 4

Streaming: the Honest Number

1T1R only completes 40% of what DDR5 completes in the same 83.33 ms matched-host window - the reported latency ratio understates the real gap.

SayThe book was updated 2026-08-23 to match this framing (compute-bound, with the 1.9-2.1x streaming penalty disclosed) - the completion panel is the point. Streaming is the weakest regime, say so plainly.
Results · Latency3 / 4

AI Inference: DDR5 Wins

  • 4.6× DDR5 under GPT-2's parallel read-storm
  • GPT-2 trace provenance unverified - treated as a stress pattern
SayNo hedging - DDR5 territory today for high-parallelism serving.
Results · Latency4 / 4

The MLC Write Tax

  • 1S1R MLC OFMAP latency ≈ 2× its SLC sibling
  • MLC → read-mostly applications only (e.g. frozen weights)
Results · Power1 / 3

The 47× Fact

  • Device-level leakage: 1T1R 795 mW/chip vs 1S1R 17 mW/chip [3]
  • For scale (not like-for-like, whole-module vendor spec): DDR5 standby floor is ≈358 mW
  • This is the number the whole power story hangs on
  • Both sides now cited: selector from HRS target [7]; transistor from ITRS 2011 + Intel's measured 22nm silicon
SayThis comes straight out of NVSim's own transistor-vs-selector access-device circuit model (Dong et al., IEEE TCAD 2012 [3]) at the 22nm FinFET LOP node - before any workload is simulated. A dedicated resistance-target sweep confirms it's the access-device model driving this, not the HRS/LRS targets (Matsui et al. [7]): leakage is bit-identical across two orders of magnitude of HRS. Both the selector-leakage and transistor-leakage inputs now trace to independent external citations; the exact 47x figure itself remains this project's own NVSim simulation, not a number published anywhere externally.
Results · Power2 / 3

Full-Module Power (Idle-Gating Restored)

  • 1T1R: 50.9 W - infeasible
  • 1S1R: 1.12 W - commodity-envelope
  • DDR5: 0.623 W (real, gated) · PCM: 0.040 W
Results · Power3 / 3

Power-Delay Product

  • 1S1R beats 1T1R by ~29-31×
  • DDR5 still ~3.7-5× ahead of ungated 1S1R
Results · Scaling1 / 2

Compute-Bound Scaling: A Real, Modest Gain

  • GCC (1T1R SLC) latency improves ~14% from 1-chip to full DIMM (152.6 → 130.9 ns)
  • Just linear leakage cost alongside it - but the latency gain itself is real, not zero
  • Root cause: address footprint, not workload parallelism - GCC's ~51 MB trace spans many memory ranks, so more ranks genuinely help
SayRoot-caused (2026-09-05): this isn't about workload MLP at all. This project's address-decode mapping gives each rank a 64 KB addressable span; GCC's trace is ~800x that size, so it genuinely spreads across every added rank. Single-chip and 8-chip are identical because both are single-rank in this architecture factory - only 16-chip and full-DIMM add real ranks. Confirmed by a dedicated queue-depth sweep that rules out a controller-queueing explanation.
Results · Scaling2 / 2

AI-Inference Is the Actual Flatline

  • GPT-2 IFMAP latency is bit-for-bit identical at every chip count (458.41 ns, 1-chip to full DIMM)
  • AlexNet IFMAP is nearly as flat (394.7 → 397.4 ns) - the highest-parallelism workloads in the suite show no scaling benefit at all
  • Root cause: both traces' ~64-68 KB working set is too small to leave a single memory rank - not an MLP story
SayRoot-caused (2026-09-05): GPT-2 IFMAP's trace touches ~64.0 KB, six bytes short of this project's exact 64 KB per-rank addressable span - every request decodes to rank 0 regardless of chip count. AlexNet IFMAP's slightly larger footprint spills a small tail into a second rank, explaining its tiny negative sensitivity. This is almost certainly an artifact of how these traces were captured (a single small SCALE-Sim layer, not a full model's working set), not evidence that AI inference in general can't benefit from rank interleaving. A dedicated queue-depth sweep rules out a controller-queueing explanation. Book's §3.2 rewritten to match; a larger AI-inference trace is future work.
Results · Viability1 / 5

Density: Architecture Decides This

  • 1S1R SLC: 1.92× DDR5 density (3.84× MLC)
  • 1T1R: 0.22× - the 20F² cell cost
  • 20F² isn't a hard ceiling - a 6F² recessed-channel demo exists
Results · Viability2 / 5

Node Scaling: Where This Could Go

  • 12-16nm + 3D deck-stacking projections
  • Bounding geometry, not measured results
Results · Viability3 / 5

Endurance

  • 8 GB (the physically simulated capacity) @ worst-case streaming: 1.1 yr - below the 5-10 yr target
  • 64 GB: ~9 yr, 128 GB: ~17 yr - both clear it, but both are a linear-scaling projection, not a separately simulated capacity (no 64 GB or 128 GB config was ever built or run)
  • Assumes ideal wear leveling - no controller implemented yet

The math: 134.2M cache-line locations × 107 rated cycles/line ≈ 1.34×1015 total writes available. LBM's 3,269,479 writes / 83.33 ms ≈ 39.2M writes/s. Budget ÷ annualized rate ≈ 1.08 yr at 8 GB - not a curve-fit, the same arithmetic scales linearly to 64/128 GB.

SayOnly 8 GB (SLC) / 16 GB (MLC) was ever actually simulated - the 64/128 GB figures are the same linear arithmetic shown above, never separately built or run.

At DDR5's spec-limit ceiling (1.008 W) the gap narrows to 1.11× - a secondary bound, not the headline.

Results · Viability5 / 5

The Path to Power Parity

Mechanism restored (DDR5 real) - ReRAM side still a projection
46%
idle time needed to break even with DDR5's restored, real 0.623 W floor
90%
idle time (plausible for web-serving deployments) → ~0.14 W, ~4.3× below DDR5's restored floor

DDR5's own idle-gating is now restored and real (0.651 → 0.623 W). ReRAM's two numbers above are still back-of-envelope arithmetic on measured static power, not a simulated gating benefit - no credible ReRAM power-gating energy figure exists in the literature (Appendix A).

Power parity only - ReRAM's separate latency verdict (Section 3.1.1) doesn't move; a workload that prioritizes latency over power should read that comparison instead, not this one.

The 90% idle case here and the Endurance slide's worst-case (sustained-write LBM) scenario are opposite ends of the workload spectrum, not the same deployment - a server idle enough for this power story would see far better real endurance than that slide's pessimistic 1.1 yr figure.

SayName ReRAM's side as a projection out loud - DDR5's own restoration is real and simulated now, which sharpens rather than resolves the parity question. Advisors respect 'here's what I haven't shown yet' far more than an unlabeled leap.

Contributions

What this delivers

Contributions1 / 2

What This Delivers

  • An open-sourced NVSim → NVMain cross-layer pipeline for ReRAM DIMM evaluation
  • A 14-item toolchain fidelity audit - reusable methodology beyond this project's own numbers
Contributions2 / 2

1S1R ReRAM is latency-competitive and density-superior today - with a credible, unproven path to power parity via idle-gating.

1T1R: a latency-only niche. High-parallelism AI serving: DDR5 territory, for now.

06
Section 06

Future Work

What would change the verdict

Future Work1 / 2

Top Priority, Next 3 Months

Idle-gating is already restored and mechanically live (Section 3.1.6). The one thing still missing: a real ReRAM power-gating characterization - what fraction of its leakage is peripheral and gatable, and at what entry/exit energy cost. That's the single highest-leverage next step, and it's a literature/analysis task, not new simulation infrastructure.

Alongside it in the same window: an Interface Parity evaluation (dual-channel / faster-PHY ReRAM) - closes part of the 4.6x AI-inference latency gap, an already-flagged available mitigation, not a hidden cost.

SayIf asked why ReRAM's power number didn't move even after idle-gating was restored: the mechanism is live (86-89% of cycle-slots gated, confirmed), but no NVSim datapoint or literature source splits ReRAM leakage into gatable-vs-ungatable, so its power-down energy is an honest zero-savings placeholder pending real characterization - exactly this priority. PCM separately shows zero power-down activity in either run, plausibly its FRFCFS-WQF controller keeping the request queue non-empty; a second, smaller open item, not yet root-caused.
Future Work2 / 2

Beyond 3 Months, by Theme

  • Architectural scaling & density - recessed-channel 1T1R density: could overturn the density verdict
  • Node scaling + 3D deck stacking, re-derived at scaled geometries
  • Macro-scale 1T1R array limits, beyond the 1024×1024 baseline-parity restriction
  • L3 cache / write-buffer mitigation for ReRAM writes
  • Endurance-aware wear-leveling at the controller level
  • Model fidelity - Native MLC Logic: resolve NVSim's Mat.cpp floating-point exception
  • PCM's zero power-down activity (FRFCFS-WQF controller) - not yet root-caused
  • Parameter optimization: ReadVoltage/WritePulseWidth sensitivity sweep
  • Validation - standalone device-to-system simulator wrapper, generalizing "The Bridge" beyond this project
  • FPGA-based hardware-in-the-loop validation of the idle-gating policy - closes the internal-only validation gap without fabricated ReRAM silicon

Thank You

Appendix - Backup

Prepare, don't present unless asked

Backup1 / 4

The Full Fidelity Audit

  • Mixed-clock-domain efficiency metric
  • Two silently ignored parameter families (leakage, access energy)
  • Technology-blind static-power default
  • Single-rank power reported as system power
  • Disabled power-down model
  • DDR5 refresh timing/supply inherited unrescaled from a DDR3 template
  • PCM baseline running at 2× its cited clock basis
  • Heterogeneous host-CPU frequencies across technologies
  • Unsourced DDR5 CAS/RCD/RP timing placeholder
  • Unsourced ReRAM MLC multipliers (one later found to carry an independent data error, also corrected)
Backup2 / 4

Design Robustness: ReadVoltage Sensitivity

  • ±20% ReadVoltage sweep around the 1.40 V design point
  • Read latency: completely invariant
  • System-level PDP: changes by <4% across the full sweep
Backup3 / 4

Worst-Case Stacking, Explained

  • DDR5 IDD figures: vendor spec-limit maxima, not typical - confirmed no typical figure exists in any datasheet checked
  • ReRAM figures: power-down mechanism now live, but an honest zero-savings placeholder pending a real gating characterization
  • DDR5 now gets a real, measured power-down credit ReRAM doesn't - the comparison no longer uniformly favors ReRAM

Most likely hard question in the room - have this ready.
